video-toilet-upgrades-and-repairs-k-84hd.title: Toilet Flange Height Solutions: Wax Seal, Shims, and a New Long-Bolt Kit (Ask This Old House)
video-toilet-upgrades-and-repairs-k-84hd.summary: This Old House’s Ask This Old House episode explains the critical seal beneath a toilet between the toilet flange and the sewer line, detailing typical components, failure modes, and practical DIY solutions for height or wobble issues. The segment covers standard configurations (closet flange, wax seal, bolts), how a floor with rot or raised grades affects sealing, and common strategies to adjust height (flange shims, plywood underlayment). It then introduces an advanced flange kit with longer bolts and integrated wax-seal hardware designed to accommodate significant up- or down- building, including a low-profile mounting method with captive fasteners and a “shock-absorber” style mechanism to preserve a positive seal during installation. The discussion highlights trade-offs, such as the potential need for a plumber for pipe modification versus DIY shim-and-kit approaches, and ends with practical tips on trimming bolts and finishing hardware.

video-toilet-upgrades-and-repairs-5nbid5.title: Toilet Tank Evolution: High-Tank (1880s) to Modern Flush Valve
video-toilet-upgrades-and-repairs-5nbid5.summary: This Old House host walks through the anatomy of a late-19th-century high-tank toilet and contrasts it with a contemporary tank, illustrating how different components functioned, why older systems were prone to failure, and how modern designs achieve reliable flushing with far less water. The discussion identifies four legacy parts (tank lever, flush valve, fill valve, and copper-walled tank with a copper tank ball float) and traces the transition to a modern flush valve with a flapper, a two-shank overflow, an adjustable fill valve, and a refill tube. The narrative explains the flow path during flush, the role of the siphon jet, and how bowl refill maintains proper water level. It also covers practical maintenance by highlighting two key adjustments—tank lever travel and float level—to ensure a one-flush, water-saving operation, including recommended target water level (about three-quarters of an inch below the overflow).

video-toilet-upgrades-and-repairs-7epc9c.title: Repair Toilet Tank Components: Flapper Replacement, Chain Adjustment, and Fill-Valve Settings
video-toilet-upgrades-and-repairs-7epc9c.summary: This This Old House segment explains how a standard toilet tank works by distinguishing the flush valve (including the flapper) from the fill valve, and then demonstrates practical repair steps to stop common leaks. The host emphasizes that leaks inside the tank waste water, and walks through identifying a worn flapper, replacing it, and adjusting the chain so the tank lever operates correctly. The video also covers setting the fill-valve height so the tank stops filling about one inch below the overflow, discusses the difference between old brass float rods and modern built-in floats, and highlights safety considerations of the overflow tube. Throughout, the emphasis is on turning off the water before work, testing after each adjustment, and avoiding over-tightening to prevent recurrent leaks.

video-toilet-upgrades-and-repairs-abox0u.title: Toilet Tank Rebuild: Replacing Fill and Flush Valves and Fine-Tuning Float
video-toilet-upgrades-and-repairs-abox0u.summary: This Old House provides a step-by-step tank-rebuild demonstration focused on diagnosing and correcting leaks in a toilet tank. The host explains the core components—the flapper/flush valve, the fill valve, the float, and the overflow tube—and how flushing and refilling work. Historical notes compare brass and copper components to modern plastic equivalents, noting that floats became integral to the valve in contemporary designs. The video then covers diagnosing a running toilet (faulty flapper seating, worn or misadjusted fill valve, or overflow-driven overfill), draining the tank, and removing the old valves. A universal repair kit is installed to replace both valves, seal the tank-to-bowl with a spud gasket, and reassemble. Final steps include positioning the refill tube, adjusting the float height, and ensuring the water level sits about one inch below the overflow to prevent leaks. The host also cautions against overtightening and provides a rough price point (~$20) for the kit.

video-toilet-upgrades-and-repairs-ip7kxv.title: How to Change a Toilet Seat (This Old House)
video-toilet-upgrades-and-repairs-ip7kxv.summary: This instructional video demonstrates the practical considerations and tools for removing and replacing a toilet seat. It covers choosing the correct seat size (round front vs elongated), exposing and removing the top bolt, and handling different hardware types—ranging from plastic wing nuts to older brass fittings. When space is tight, it introduces specialized tools such as a basin wrench and a ratcheting adjustable wrench, and it discusses strategies for stubborn or corroded bolts, including penetrating oil, deep sockets, cutting the bolt with a hacksaw, and protecting the porcelain with a putty/ broad knife to avoid damage. The presenter emphasizes adapting the approach to the hardware and space constraints rather than following a single universal method.

video-toilet-upgrades-and-repairs-jma8hu.title: Converting a Toilet to Dual-Flush: Retrofit, Valve Installation, and Bowl Refilling
video-toilet-upgrades-and-repairs-jma8hu.summary: This Old House walks a homeowner through converting an existing 3.5 gallons-per-flush toilet into a dual-flush model using a retrofit valve and a two-button actuator. The video covers removing the old tank lever, installing a dual-flush valve with a blue gasket, attaching a two-button actuator (one for liquids, one for solids), and reconfiguring the fill valve to ensure the bowl refills adequately after a reduced liquid flush. The host demonstrates turning off the water, draining the tank, wiring and securing components, and then testing a liquid flush that uses significantly less water while preserving a full flush for solids. A noted tradeoff is that the bowl needs adequate refill water, prompting a later adjustment with an adjustable fill valve and refill tube to restore proper bowl performance. The segment ends with a recap of how to use the top (liquids) and bottom (solids) buttons and the expected water savings.

video-toilet-upgrades-and-repairs-lcpdub.title: Graywater Toilet Retrofit: Integrated Hand-Wash Sink Demonstration
video-toilet-upgrades-and-repairs-lcpdub.summary: This This Old House video presents a retrofit approach to turn a standard toilet into a graywater-capable unit by adding an integrated hand-wash sink above the tank. The host first explains the normal operation of a toilet tank (flapper, fill valve, refill tube) and notes that both the tank refill water and the bowl refill water are clean. The demonstration then shows a retrofit kit that replaces the refill tube with a clear plastic tube to divert water to a top device and toward the bowl, enabling a hand-washing sink to receive clean water after flushing. A spacer is introduced to accommodate different tank lengths. The clip concludes with the claim that the kit can be installed on standard toilets to provide a dedicated hand-washing sink while maintaining the standard bowl refill cycle. The product is described as originating from Australia and is marketed as a retrofit option available in the United States.

video-toilet-upgrades-and-repairs-lngdzk.title: Noisy Toilet Repair: Flush Valve Replacement and Tank Reassembly (This Old House)
video-toilet-upgrades-and-repairs-lngdzk.summary: A This Old House segment diagnosing a noisy toilet guides viewers through identifying a faulty flush valve as the noise source, explains the age and design of a 1990s-era low-flow toilet, and then demonstrates a full valve replacement. The host walks through turning off water, draining and removing the tank from the bowl, replacing the flush valve and associated gaskets and hardware, and reassembling with careful adjustments to chain length, refill tube placement, water level, and flush volume. The episode concludes with notes on balancing performance and water conservation, noting that the result is effectively a brand-new toilet built from standard modern components.

video-toilet-upgrades-and-repairs-nlrh7j.title: How to Install a Dual-Flush Toilet (Skirted) — Mounting, Wax Seal, Tank, and Water Connection
video-toilet-upgrades-and-repairs-nlrh7j.summary: This Old House demonstrates installing a skirted, dual-flush toilet, including discussion of dual-flush operation (0.9 gpf for liquids and 1.6 gpf for solids) and a concealed mounting system. The video walks through removing the old wax seal and bolts, using a manufacturer template to place mounting blocks, drilling through tile and into wood, installing mounting hardware and a wax ring, dropping the toilet into place, securing it with brass screws and chrome caps, and assembling the tank to the bowl with a gasket and bolts. It then covers connecting the water supply and refill tube, reinstalling the flush valve, turning the water back on, and placing the tank top. The transcript notes practical tips such as keeping the wax seal at room temperature for compression and using a sharp masonry bit for tile work.

video-toilet-upgrades-and-repairs-ojsbqh.title: How to Repair a Leaking Toilet: Wax Rings, Flange Height, and Spacers
video-toilet-upgrades-and-repairs-ojsbqh.summary: This Old House's Ask This Old House episode guides diagnosing a leaking toilet by examining common leak sources (water-supply connections, tank-to-bowl gasket, and flange seals), explains the wax ring’s role and how floor instability can deform it, and presents modern height-adjustment options (foam gaskets and flange spacers) to restore a proper seal. The host emphasizes securing the flange to structural supports, accurately restoring flange height to finish-floor level, and finally returning to a conventional wax seal once the height is correct, to achieve a durable, non-rocking installation.

The speaker notes the flange’s height relative to the old floor, removes and replaces the brittle cast-iron piece, aligns bolts, installs the wax ring, and completes the assembly with the toilet mounted and tested for wobble and leaks.

video-toilet-upgrades-and-repairs-tatkoj.title: Installing a Below-Grade Toilet with a Macerator Pump (This Old House)
video-toilet-upgrades-and-repairs-tatkoj.summary: This Old House demonstrates installing a toilet below grade using a macerator unit behind the toilet. The video contrasts a standard siphon-jet toilet with a P-trap style discharge fed by a macerator, explains how waste is pumped through a small-diameter line to tie into the house drain, covers venting to the vent stack, and shows the practical steps of rough-in, priming and cementing PVC joints, securing the fixture to the subfloor with brass lag screws, connecting the toilet to the macerator with a rubber gasket and clamps, and finally restoring the water supply to test the tank fill.

video-toilet-upgrades-and-repairs-wki3nc.title: Repairing a Rotted Cast-Iron Toilet Flange with a Retrofit Gasket and Spacer System
video-toilet-upgrades-and-repairs-wki3nc.summary: This Old House’s tutorial walks through diagnosing a leak tied to a failed wax seal and a rotted cast-iron closet flange after a bathroom remodel. The host explains toilet anatomy (trapway, siphon jet, and flange), identifies a downstroom stoppage as the likely leak cause, then shuts off water and removes the toilet. A remodel revealed the old cast-iron flange was missing or severely degraded, prompting a retrofit approach: replace with a gasket-style flange adapter designed for cast-iron pipe, using spacers to set the correct height, and switching from a traditional wax seal to a flexible gasket. The video covers removing corroded bolts with a mini-hacksaw, reassembling with new closet bolts and washers, and confirming a leak-free connection after restoring water supply.

video-toilet-upgrades-and-repairs-wm-6bg.title: How to Install a New Toilet: Shutoffs, Flange Prep, and Wax Ring Assembly
video-toilet-upgrades-and-repairs-wm-6bg.summary: This video progressively demonstrates a full toilet install in a residential bathroom: shutting off the main water, adding a service shut-off, trimming and configuring copper supply piping, preparing and securing the drain line with a closet flange, removing old installation material, and mounting a new two-piece toilet with gasket, bolts, wax ring, and a flexible water-supply line. It covers measuring flange height, shortening the drain pipe via a drill/cutter, anchoring the flange, installing the wax seal, mounting the toilet, trimming bolts, and performing a water-test flush to confirm leak-free operation.

video-toilet-upgrades-and-repairs-y2o8up.title: How a Plumbing Trap Can Lose Water: Traps, Vents, and Common Causes
video-toilet-upgrades-and-repairs-y2o8up.summary: This Old House explains how a washing machine drain can pull water out of a toilet trap when a vent is absent or clogged, by using a mock-up to illustrate traps and water seals. The video defines key plumbing elements—P-traps, toilet traps, and vent pipes—and demonstrates how a vent allows air into the drainage system to prevent negative pressure and gurgling. It contrasts unvented versus vented drain conditions, discusses where vents should connect, and covers several mechanisms that can cause trap seals to fail, including oscillation from wind, siphonage with S-traps, capillary action, evaporation, and momentum. The host offers practical notes on checking vents, considering mechanical vent options, and refilling traps if sewer gas smells occur.
